title: Hydrated minerals (CRISM HYD, scene FRT0000B6F1)

legend.label: Magenta: polyhydrated sulfates
Yellow to green: monohydrated sulfates
Blue: other hydrated minerals (clays, glass, carbonate, zeolite)

legend_note: Verified. red = SINDEX2, spectral index keyed to bound water bands indicative of hydrated sulfates; green = BD2100_2, 2100 nm band depth attributable to a shifted H2O band exhibited by monohydrated sulfates; blue = BD1900_2, 1900 nm band depth attributable to bound molecular H2O. Polyhydrated sulfates have strong 1900 nm and 2400 nm bands and appear magenta; monohydrated sulfates have a strong 2100 nm band and appear yellow/green; blue indicates other hydrated minerals (such as clays, glass, carbonate or zeolite). Band names are from this file's PDS label (https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/mro/mro-m-crism-5-rdr-mptargeted-v1/mrocr_4001/browse/2008/2008_191/frt0000b6f1/frt0000b6f1_07_brhydj_mtr3.lbl); the wording is from the CRISM Data Product SIS v1.3.7.7, list of browse products (https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/mro/mro-m-crism-5-rdr-mptargeted-v1/mrocr_4001/document/crism_dpsis.htm), which cites Viviano-Beck et al. 2014. Colours show the relative strength of spectral bands inside this one scene, not amounts of a mineral, and are not comparable between scenes: each scene has its own stretch. The label says spectra must be analysed for a positive mineral identification.
source: MRO CRISM map-projected targeted reduced data record (MTRDR) browse product FRT0000B6F1_07_BRHYDJ_MTR3, PDS Geosciences Node
notes: MRO CRISM scene FRT0000B6F1, acquired 2008-07-09. Cropped to the map box from 775 x 714 to 528 x 615 pixels; 96% of the cropped image has data, the rest is transparent. 957 of 1388 rover stops fall on a valid pixel (sols 1448 to 5070). bounds_label are the pixel outer edges worked out from the PDS label. With those bounds the scene sits off the HiRISE base map, so 'bounds' are moved 193 m west and 71 m north (measured, see 'registration'; correlation 0.64 after the move, -0.19 before). The two halves of the scene differ from this single shift by up to about 59 m, so expect that much error in places. The pixels are not resampled.

title: Iron minerals (CRISM FM2, scene FRT0000B6F1)

legend.label: Red: nanophase ferric oxides (530 nm band)
Green: coarser-grained iron minerals or low-Ca pyroxene (920 nm band)
Blue: dust-free or more mafic surfaces (1000 nm band)

legend_note: Verified. red = BD530_2, 530 nm band depth indicating the presence of nanophase ferric oxides; green = BD920_2, 920 nm band depth highlighting coarser-grained ferric minerals or low-Ca pyroxene; blue = BDI1000VIS, 1000 nm VNIR band depth highlighting dust-free or more mafic surfaces. Particularly sensitive to olivine and pyroxene, as well as nanophase ferric oxide and crystalline ferric or ferrous minerals. Red often indicates nanophase ferric oxides, green coarser-grained iron-bearing minerals, blue dust-free or more mafic surfaces. The SIS table of summary parameters adds for the red band (BD530_2): higher value has more crystalline hematite. The label says spectra must be analysed for a positive mineral identification.

legend_note: Brightness is the daytime infrared mosaic (landforms); colour is the night-time infrared mosaic (relative night temperature), as the layer's title and abstract in the JMARS WMS capabilities say. The colour ramp itself is not documented by the service. Ground that stays warm at night is usually rock or cemented ground, ground that cools fast is usually loose sand or dust. Relative temperatures only, no kelvin values. Checked here against the thermal inertia layer: hue runs from red (high thermal inertia, warm at night) through yellow and green to blue (low, cold at night); correlation of hue angle with thermal inertia over the box is -0.88. Legend colours are nominal, not sampled.
source: ASU JMARS WMS, THEMIS Day IR with Colorized Night IR 100 m global mosaic v13.4 (thm_dirnir_100m_v13_4)
notes: Requested at 388 x 800 pixels, about four times finer than the 100 m data, so the server's own resampling does the smoothing. One real pixel is about the size of a football field. Position: bounds are the requested box, not adjusted. A one-off check against the elevation grid suggests the daytime infrared mosaic sits roughly 200 m (two of its own pixels) north of the HiRISE base map; the night-time mosaic and the thermal inertia were not testable. Treat positions as good to a few hundred metres.

legend.label: Red: warmest at night: rock or cemented ground (mean 568 TIU here)
Orange to yellow: warm (mean 441 TIU here)
Green: cool: looser ground (mean 324 TIU here)
Cyan to blue: coldest at night: loose sand or dust (mean 242 TIU here)

title: Thermal inertia (THEMIS)
legend_note: Pixel value p stands for 210 + p * (710 - 210) / 255 TIU. Low thermal inertia means loose, fine material such as sand or dust; high means rock or cemented ground. The app's loose-ground stipple uses the same data with limits at 300 and 400 TIU.
source: ASU JMARS WMS, THEMIS Quantitative Thermal Inertia 100 m Global Mosaic, 32-bit (thm_ti_100m_32bit)
notes: Data in the box run from 210 to 707 TIU. Quantised in steps of 2.0 TIU (largest rounding error 0.98 TIU). 0 of 77600 cells have no data. Requested at 194 x 400 cells, about twice finer than the 100 m data. Plain 8-bit grey, no alpha. Read pixel values from a canvas with image smoothing off. Position: bounds are the requested box, not adjusted. A one-off check against the elevation grid suggests the daytime infrared mosaic sits roughly 200 m (two of its own pixels) north of the HiRISE base map; the night-time mosaic and the thermal inertia were not testable. Treat positions as good to a few hundred metres.
